title: ARQUE Systems and Forschungszentrum Jülich Plan 200-Qubit Quantum Computer
html:
Insider Brief

  • ARQUE Systems and Forschungszentrum Jülich are developing a semiconductor-based quantum computer with up to 200 qubits under the €35 million Q-STAR.NRW project.
  • The system uses electron-spin qubits in silicon and silicon-germanium structures, with a shuttling technique designed to move quantum information across the chip and reduce control-line requirements.
  • The project runs until the end of 2029 and will integrate the quantum computer into Jülich’s JUNIQ infrastructure alongside classical high-performance computing resources.

PRESS RELEASE — ARQUE Systems, a Jülich–Aachen spin-off, aims to overcome a major hurdle in quantum computing using innovative quantum semiconductor technology. As part of the € 35 million Q-STAR.NRW project, their approach will now be tested with up to 200 qubits, helping to stimulate value creation in the Rhenish mining area.

The development of quantum computers faces major technological challenges. In future, systems containing a very large numbers of qubits will be required for complex applications in materials research, chemistry, logistics, and process optimization. Taking into account the additional effort required for error correction, this demand could rise to hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of physical qubits. Scalability is therefore a crucial prerequisite for the development of such high-performance systems.

This is where ARQUE Systems comes in. The deep-tech start-up, a spin-off from Forschungszentrum Jülich and RWTH Aachen University, is pursuing a patented technological approach that draws on established semiconductor technology. This technology already enables billions of transistors to be integrated onto a single computer chip.

ARQUE Systems recently demonstrated the fundamental feasibility of this approach by integrating a five-qubit quantum computer into the Jülich UNified Infrastructure for Quantum Computing (JUNIQ). The next step is now set to follow. As part of the Q-STAR.NRW project, Forschungszentrum Jülich and ARQUE Systems aim to ensure that the technology also functions reliably on a larger scale. The plan is to build a quantum computer with up to 200 qubits. The project will run until the end of 2029 and has a total funding volume of around € 35 million.

Prof. Dr. Astrid Lambrecht, Chair of the Board of Directors of Forschungszentrum Jülich:

Q-STAR.NRW is an excellent example of how at Forschungszentrum Jülich, we combine scientific excellence, technology transfer, and practical application. At Jülich, we bring together cutting-edge research, unique research infrastructures, and strong industry partners to translate scientific findings into technological innovations. With Q-STAR.NRW, we are developing a semiconductor-based quantum computing technology that, through its integration into JUNIQ, will extend its impact far beyond Jülich, while also providing important impetus for the Rhenish mining area and North Rhine-Westphalia as a technology hub.

Movable qubits as the key to scalability

ARQUE Systems’ technological approach combines two advantages: the miniaturization potential of established semiconductor technology and a patent-pending method for the targeted transport of quantum information.

The qubits are based on the spin of individual electrons in silicon and silicon–germanium structures. They can be switched rapidly, are particularly small, and use materials and manufacturing approaches that are well established in the semiconductor industry. This means that potentially very large numbers of qubits can be integrated onto a single chip. In the long term, this approach could enable more than ten million qubits to be integrated onto a chip measuring approximately two by two centimetres.

The key innovation, however, lies in the mobility of the qubits. In the patented shuttling process, electrons and their quantum information are transported in a controlled manner across the chip. This solves several challenges at once: qubits no longer need to be arranged next to one another permanently to enable coupling. It is also no longer necessary to control each individual qubit via its own signal line. Instead, the electrons can be moved to specific locations on the chip where they interact with one another and enable quantum operations.

This simplified control architecture and the significantly reduced number of control lines create the conditions for realizing quantum chips with substantially larger numbers of qubits.

Prof. Dr. Kristel Michielsen, Director at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre:

With Q-STAR.NRW, we are taking the next important step in integrating quantum computing into our European high-performance computing infrastructures. It is crucial that we do not view quantum computers as isolated systems, but instead integrate them closely with classical supercomputers and enable their use in real-world scientific and industrial applications. Integrating the new semiconductor-based system into JUNIQ allows us to develop hybrid quantum-HPC workflows on a powerful and scalable platform and make them accessible to a broad user community.

From quantum chip to usable infrastructure

The new quantum computer will be integrated into the Jülich UNified Infrastructure for Quantum Computing (JUNIQ) at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre (JSC), where it will be connected to classical high-performance computers and made available to users from science and industry. These users will be able to develop and test new applications under real-world conditions and, in the longer term, translate them into industrial use.

The project partners are developing not only the hardware but also the necessary software, hybrid quantum algorithms, and services for user support and training.

Dr. Markus Beckers, CEO of ARQUE Systems GmbH:

For ARQUE Systems, Q-STAR.NRW is about much more than building a single quantum computer. Together with Forschungszentrum Jülich, we want to demonstrate that scalable, semiconductor-based quantum computing can be developed in North Rhine-Westphalia and integrated into a world-leading computing infrastructure. We believe that the combination of shuttling technology, semiconductor expertise, quantum computing, and supercomputing offers an exceptional opportunity to develop a truly scalable technology platform. We are very proud to be taking this next step together with our partners.

New technology and value creation for the Rhenish mining area

Q-STAR.NRW marks an important milestone for quantum computing in North Rhine-Westphalia, while also contributing to industrial structural change in the Rhenish mining area.

The project receives 90 % of its funding from federal funds under the Coal Regions Investment Act (InvKG). The remaining 10 % contribution from Forschungszentrum Jülich is funded entirely by the State of North Rhine-Westphalia.

The infrastructure being developed will be particularly open to small and medium-sized enterprises. This will enable them to explore new applications in areas such as materials development, chemistry, pharmaceuticals, logistics, and industrial optimization at an early stage, without having to bear the investment and technological risks associated with having their own infrastructure.

From coal to high tech

In future, an ecosystem could develop around the new infrastructure, bringing together the research community, start-ups, established companies, suppliers, and educational institutions. The project will thus help to promote collaboration, encourage further spin-offs, and attract businesses to the region. The long-term aim is to develop the Rhenish mining area and North Rhine-Westphalia into an internationally recognized European hub for applied quantum computing and future computing, while also creating new industrial value in the Rhenish mining area.

Mona Neubaur, Minister of Economic Affairs, Industry, Climate Action and Energy of the State of North Rhine-Westphalia:

A sovereign Europe needs technological strength – and that is what we are creating here in the Rhenish mining area. Quantum technologies are among the most exciting and promising technologies of our time, as they offer enormous opportunities for fast and secure digital processes and intelligent solutions to the major challenges of our times. Here, cutting-edge technology is being developed that benefits many companies in the chemical, pharmaceutical, and logistics sectors – and, through their products, everyone.

Mohib Ur Rehman

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

Arque's mission is to develop and commercialize Quantum Computing systems reaching beyond current capabilities based on electron spins in silicon.

Forschungszentrum Jülich (FZJ) is one of the largest interdisciplinary research institutions in Europe, focusing on energy, information, and bioeconomy. Located in Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, it employs approximately 7,250 staff members, including many international researchers. FZJ operates advanced scientific infrastructures, such as supercomputers and particle accelerators, and conducts research aimed at addressing major societal challenges, including climate change and sustainable resource management. As a member of the Helmholtz Association, it collaborates with over 200 partners globally, fostering innovation in various fields through interdisciplinary approaches and cutting-edge technologies.
